alt: Article 11.1, a qualified right, splits into peaceful assembly (meeting in public or private: marches, static protests, rallies, sit-ins) and association with others (formal or lasting groups, including trade unions, political parties and campaign groups). A note explains that a protest usually expresses an opinion, so Article 11 is read in the light of Article 10.
caption: Assembly and association: two linked freedoms, both read alongside Article 10.

alt: Three situations. If organisers or participants intend violence the assembly falls outside Article 11. A person who stays peaceful while others are violent is still protected (Ezelin v France, breach). A disruptive protest is still peaceful (Kudrevičius v Lithuania), though deliberate serious disruption is not at the core of the freedom and the convictions were justified.
caption: Violent intention removes protection; disruption or other people’s violence does not.

alt: Two panels. Private land: Appleby v UK found no breach when campaigners were stopped in a privately owned shopping centre because they had other ways to reach the public. Public highway: DPP v Jones held a peaceful, non-obstructive assembly can be a reasonable use, and DPP v Ziegler required a proportionality assessment of lawful excuse, restoring the protesters’ acquittals.
caption: No right to use private land where alternatives exist; the highway can be used peacefully.

alt: Three points. Plattform Ärzte für das Leben v Austria: states must take reasonable and appropriate measures to protect lawful demonstrations, a duty of means not results. Laporte: turning back protesters’ coaches was unlawful because a breach of the peace was not imminent and the action was disproportionate. Kay: section 11 of the Public Order Act 1986 exempts processions commonly or customarily held, such as Critical Mass.
caption: The state must protect peaceful protest and needs clear, proportionate grounds to stop it.

alt: A table of six association cases. Trade unions: Young, James and Webster (a negative freedom not to be forced to join), ASLEF (breach, a union may choose its members), the rail union case (no breach, wide margin). Political association: Redfearn (UK failed its positive obligation), United Communist Party of Turkey (dissolution a breach) and Refah Partisi (dissolution justified).
caption: Association covers the freedom not to join and a union’s freedom to choose its members.

alt: The nurses’ vigil in five steps: Article 11.1 read with Article 10; the nurses stay peaceful despite others’ violence (Ezelin); the pavement is highway that can be used peacefully (DPP v Jones); police have a duty to protect the vigil (Plattform); Kim’s arrest needs justification, compared with Laporte, and Article 11.2 decides.
caption: Peaceful, lawful location, positive duty: then test the arrest under Article 11.2.
